facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
The applicants in the Chrysostomos and Papachrysostomou v. Turkey and Loizidou v. Turkey cases also took part in the anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia on 19 July 1989.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court on 7 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court on 7 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held on the fifteenth anniversary of the Turkish intervention in Cyprus.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court on 7 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held in support of the missing persons and to protest against human-rights violations.
The applicant decided to go to the area where the events of 19 July 1989 were taking place.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment on 19 July 1989.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters and were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that before the District Court gave its sentence, the Bishop of Kitium, speaking on behalf of all the accused, made a statement saying that their struggle had been peaceful, that their aim was to have Greek-Cypriots and Turkish-Cypriots living together in peace, that they had not been carrying weapons and that they had asked for UN protection.
While the applicant was trying to attend to the injured woman, he was beaten with clubs about the head and body by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
The applicant was led away at gunpoint through an angry crowd that shouted abuse and threats on 19 July 1989.
The applicant was taken by bus to the so-called 'Pavlides Garage' on 19 July 1989.
In the morning of 20 July 1989, the applicant was taken to Seray Police Station and put in a cell that was dark, damp and dirty.
The applicant was remanded in custody for two days after the court appearance on 20 July 1989.

On 22 July 1989, the applicant was sentenced to three days' imprisonment and a fine of 50 Cyprus pounds (approximately 85 euros), with five additional days in prison in default of payment within 24 hours.
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.
The Government alleged that the applicant was charged, tried, found guilty and sentenced to a short term of imprisonment.

The English translation of the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory without permission, contrary to sections 2, 8 and 9 of Law no. 5/72.

The English translation of the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory other than through an approved port, contrary to subsections 12(1) and (5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorization, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment on 19 July 1989.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators, supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration, were demanding that the 'Green Line' in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters and were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by UNFICYP and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the events of 19 July 1989 created considerable tension in the island and intensive efforts were made, both at the UN headquarters and at Nicosia, to contain and resolve the situation.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that the prosecution witnesses (mainly police officers on duty at the time of the demonstration) declared that the accused had illegally crossed the 'TRNC' border, shouted abuse at the Turkish-Cypriot forces and resisted arrest by pulling and pushing.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court concluded, relying on statements by the prosecution witnesses, that the accused had crossed the borders of the 'TRNC' at an unapproved entry point and without permission and had resisted by various means the UN and Turkish forces which had tried to stop them.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court on 7 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
The applicant was a nursing officer.
The applicant took with him a special bag containing first-aid equipment when he went to the demonstration area on 19 July 1989.
The applicant wore an armband marked with the Red Cross sign when he went to the demonstration area on 19 July 1989.
The applicant told UN officers that he was a nurse on 19 July 1989.
UN officers informed the applicant that they needed his help for a woman who had received an injury to the head and was lying on the ground.
While the applicant was trying to attend to the injured woman, he was beaten with clubs about the head and body by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
Despite the applicant's attempts to explain that he was a nurse, Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control continued to hit him.
The applicant informed the judge on 20 July 1989 that he had attended the demonstration only in order to offer humanitarian aid as a member of the Red Cross.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the 'TRNC'.
The Government alleged that no force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the 'TRNC' border area on 19 July 1989.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
In photographs 8 to 10 produced by the applicant, members of the Turkish-Cypriot police are seen breaking up the UNFICYP cordon during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The final set of photographs produced by the applicant show members of the Turkish-Cypriot police using force to arrest some of the demonstrators during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that the prosecution witnesses (mainly police officers on duty at the time of the demonstration) declared that the accused had illegally crossed the 'TRNC' border, shouted abuse at the Turkish-Cypriot forces and resisted arrest by pulling and pushing.
The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that knives and other cutting objects had been found in the bags of some of the demonstrators who had been arrested.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court concluded, relying on statements by the prosecution witnesses, that the accused had crossed the borders of the 'TRNC' at an unapproved entry point and without permission and had resisted by various means the UN and Turkish forces which had tried to stop them.

In deciding on the sentence, the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court took into account the seriousness of the offence and the fact that the accused had shown no remorse and continued to deny the validity of the 'TRNC'.
